newsitem.title: UK: London's Hyde Park could grow east under new plan.
newsitem.headline: London's Hyde Park could grow east under new plan.

text.p: A 100 million pound ($165 million) proposal was unveiled on Wednesday to extend London's Hyde Park, submerge a busy road in a tunnel and create a piazza in front of Marble Arch.

The consortium behind the project, which is still at the concept stage, includes Grosvenor Estate Holdings, headed by the Duke of Westminster, one of Britain's wealthiest men and the owner of prime sites to the east of the park.
The scheme has the backing of the Royal Parks Agency, which manages Hyde Park, central London's biggest.
The park stands to regain at least the six acres (2.4 hectares) it lost with the widening of Park Lane in 1958, Royal Parks chief executive David Welch told a news conference.

Tourists and Londoners alike would benefit, he said. "At present Marble Arch is isolated on a traffic-choked roundabout, and beneath it Londoners are cast into troglodytic misery in gloomy grey (pedestrian) tunnels," he said.
The top hotels and businesses on the east side of Park Lane would benefit from reduced traffic and the new vista opened up.
The warren of underground pedestrian walkways linking Hyde Park to Marble Arch and Oxford Street, the capital's main shopping street, would disappear.

Instead, pedestrians would have a pleasant stroll over the piazza and landscaped parkland which would replace the northbound lanes of Park Lane, a busy road linking the western end of Oxford Street with Piccadilly, Mayfair and Knightsbridge.

The southbound lanes would be used by buses and local traffic going in both directions, while the rest of the vehicles that currently use Park Lane would travel through a new, four-lane underground tunnel.
The "multicoloured steel wall of tourist coaches" that line the west side of Park Lane most days would be sent to an at present under-utilised underground car park, Welch said.
Designers said the project faced several hurdles.

In particular, a public inquiry would have to be held and parliamentary legislation would be needed. That would probably take around three years, and building work would need another two to three years, giving a possible completion date of 2002. ($1=.6072 Pound)
